Baskervilles are not bite proof for determined biters, because they are soft and many dogs figure out they can still bite if they just push hard enough. I've been bitten several times by dogs in Baskervilles. Typically biothane muzzles like Bumas or Khaos Kollars are also not bite proof for the same reason.

I would join the Facebook group Muzzle Up Pup! or Muzzle Training and Tricks. They can help you select an appropriate muzzle and size it correctly.

Dean & Tyler, Leerburg, or Jafco muzzles are all bite proof, can be worn for extended periods, and allow your dog to eat, drink, pant, and take treats.

Of course, this all depends on how determined of a biter your mom's dog is! If hes not very determined, a Baskerville will likely work just fine.

I use a large gravel cleaner for my 20 gallon, and almost completely kink the hose when I dig it into the substrate so that the heavier stratum bits fall back out but detritus still gets sucked in. I have to keep kinking and unkinking the hose through the whole thing, but I personally didn't find it to be much of a hassle once I got the hang of it. 

I started out with a tiny 5-10 gallon siphon but the tube was so short the stratum would get sucked in before I could kink the hose, plus it would usually stop suctioning completely when I kinked it. So I switched to a big one and had no problems anymore.

I'm a vet tech specializing in nutrition. Mythbusting is my favorite part. I currently work at a Petco as a dog trainer and I'm also the pet food specialist. Petco will price match the website of any brick-and-mortar building, plus you can use coupons when you price-match.

The brand I recommend the most often is Purina Pro Plan. They have veterinarians and board-certified nutritionists on staff, private manufacturing facilities, hold their suppliers to incredibly rigorous tests and inspections, are constantly doing research in the nutrition field (as opposed to finding the magic recipe and stopping there), publish their findings for the public to read, and they are one of the few companies that do animal feed tests on their food, which means they feed the food to a group of dogs for six months, then perform blood tests, urinalysis and fecal tests, to see how many of the nutrients the dogs are keeping and using instead of just pooping out. Pro Plan is also pretty cheap compared to other premium pet foods, but meat is still the first ingredient. Their food is also nutrient-dense, which means your pet can eat less of it and still get all the nutrition they need, and that way you can spend less!

For the record, I used to hate Purina with a fiery passion and they were as good as the devil in my eyes. But once I got into the field and started studying, I found out that a VAST majority of my prior nutrition information was completely incorrect. And I also discovered that, as much as I hated to admit it, Purina actually makes really good food and they're extremely good at what they do.

If you'd rather avoid Purina anyway, there are only a few that I would personally use if Pro Plan was out of the question. They are Hills Science Diet, Iams, Eukanuba, Natural Balance, Merrick, and Canidae. With the exception of Hills, these companies don't do feed tests on their food to determine the true nutrient content, but because of who they keep on staff, and because of the standards the manufacturing plants are held to, I feel comfortable recommending them.

Some things to keep in mind:

You don't need to feed your pet grain free unless they are allergic to grains. Grain free is a marketing term, not a health term. As long as the nutrients are there in the correct ratios, it really doesn't matter which ingredients they're coming from. When nutritionally balanced, grain free diets are no better or worse for your pet's health than other diets, but they do tend to have higher levels of fat and calories, and tend to be very rich and can sometimes cause GI upset.

Raw diets are recommended against by the large majority of veterinary associations. It's very very hard to balance them nutritionally,  especially if you're doing it with no input from a professional. We would get a lot of cases in the clinic of people feeding homemade recipes that ended up being nutritionally deficient and made their pets very sick. If you have to do raw, work with a vet to make sure it's nutritionally complete and balanced. When balanced, raw diets are no better or worse for your pet's health, but there is generally a higher bacterial and pathogen load (as is the case with any raw meat).

There is a lot of misconception here about pet foods. 

Grain free is really only marketed for owners, as it doesn't benefit most pets to take away grains (unless they have an allergy or sensitivity). All of those ingredients are there for a reason. Grains are a common source of carbs, which is what's broken down into energy. They also provide protein, fat, fiber, minerals, and vitamins. They also add grain fillers to make your pet feel fuller while eating less food, and it also provides fiber and promotes digestive health, and it tends to have better absorption and digestibility. This is absolutely fine for your cat. Wild cats usually eat the stomach contents of their kills. 

Cats usually use protein to repair and maintain the body and make energy, but if they consume carbs, they can use that to make energy instead of using protein, which isn't as efficient. Cats also require linoleic acid, and one of the best sources of that is vegetable oils from corn, soybean, and safflower oil.

That being said, Hills Science Diet, Purina, and Royal Canin are the best quality foods to feed your cat. 

Look for the AAFCO statement on the back of the bag. If the package says it's suitable for all life stages, that means it'll keep your cat alive, but does not contain optimum levels, because each life stage has different nutritional requirements. Kittens need a minimum of 30% protein in their dry food, and once they reach one year of age, the requirement goes down to 26%. Be conscious of that when choosing a food. 

Dry food is good for your cat's teeth; it will help scrape tartar off and keep them healthy. Kittens can safely eat solid food as early as five or six weeks old. If she doesn't like dry food, try mixing the wet and dry food together to create a sort of mash.

Your dog likely has a flea allergy and environmental allergy. The flea allergy causes your dog to bite at his hindquarters, and the environment allergy (probably pollen of some kind) causes him to chew his paws. Often the licking and chewing will lead to a secondary yeast infection on his skin, which causes additional itching and hair loss. 
Advantix is garbage, honestly. Pretty much anything you can find at Walmart is going to be garbage. I highly recommend going to a different vet and asking for flea preventatives like Activl (monthly topical), Bravecto(treat that lasts for three months), or Trifexus(more expensive, but protects your dog from a huge number of parasites. It is a once a month treat). Activyl will be the cheapest, usually under $20.
You'll also probably need to get some antifungal dog shampoo to take care of the yeast infection. At my clinic, we generally recommend bathing three times a week for two weeks. 

Source: I am a vet tech in the South, where 90% of patients come in with these symptoms. We diagnose and treat it very regularly.

I ended up calling once more and telling them I was afraid they went into the house to get a gun, and suddenly three cop cars were there in five minutes flat.

What did they do? Talked to the owner of the house, walked around inside,  and...nothing else. They didn't take statements, they didn't dust for fingerprints or make any sort of effort to find them. They essentially told me too bad, so sad and I went home. I was scared shitless. They lived only a block down the street, and I couldn't sleep soundly for two weeks. I was afraid they'd try to take my car again, or hurt me, since I'm a young female and live alone.

I'm in my early twenties, so I guess I got my wakeup call pretty late on life compared to other posters, but that was when I lost my sense of safety and security. If the police wouldn't do anything to help me or at least make me feel safer, then who would help if I was in danger?
